newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's new Europe minister is key Jospin ally.
newsitem.headline: France's new Europe minister is key Jospin ally.

text.p: Socialist Pierre Moscovici, a skilled technocrat and aide to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, was named European affairs minister on Wednesday, taking on the issue of European Union institutional reform just two weeks before a key summit in Amsterdam.

Moscovici, 39, one of the authors of the Socialist party's economic policy, was described by a right-wing opponent during the campaign for Sunday's parliamentary election as Jospin's "strong right arm".
He will need that strength to manage relations with France's European partners and with conservative President Jacques Chirac, who will want to keep a big say in European policy.

His predecessor, Gaullist Michel Barnier, was also France's representative at the Intergovernmental Conference negotiations on EU reform. It was not immediately clear if Moscovici would inherit that role.
The talks are now in the final throes, with such important questions as the weighting of member-states' votes in majority decisions still to be agreed.

A 1984 graduate of France's elite Ecole Nationale d'Administration, Moscovici is credited with being the first to alert Jospin to the risk that Chirac might dissolve parliament, giving the opposition Socialists much-needed time to mobilise for a surprise campaign.
Moscovici advises Jospin partly by bombarding him with economic policy notes and heads a virtual "shadow cabinet" made up of young Socialist economic policy experts.

He played a critical role in attracting a new generation of economists, technocrats and young corporate chiefs to the Socialist fold after the 1993 election debacle, which saw the left buried under a landslide conservative victory.
Moscovici won a seat in parliament last Sunday for the eastern city of Montbeliard, near the Swiss border.
He holds several advanced degrees in politics and economics, including a degree from the Institut d'Etudes Politique, the famed Sciences Po, in Paris.
